Plus, bond rout continues and Elon eyes turbine parts

U.S. stocks look set to open lower with index futures down, though they don’t yet appear poised to repeat yesterday’s sharp declines.

Going all in

 

Broadcom might be the biggest winner from the AI-chip craze after Nvidia, with a growing roster of large customers and $100 billion of revenue projected for that segment of its business in its next fiscal year.

 

But Broadcom, which reports results later today, is also beset with competitive and technical challenges. And as it becomes a more concentrated bet on AI chips, it loses some appeal to investors as a more diversified play.

 

Broadcom came into the AI boom as a hodgepodge of chip and software businesses assembled by Chief Executive Hock Tan. Those businesses weren’t fast growing, at least by AI-boom standards. But they brought healthy profit margins that Tan ruthlessly sought to improve.

 

Google changed the game at the boom’s outset. The search giant had been codeveloping customized AI chips, called tensor processing units, with Broadcom for some time before AI took off. When Microsoft started infusing its Bing search engine with AI, Google saw a threat to its core ad business and ordered as many AI chips as it could. Broadcom was off to the races.

 

Similar custom AI-chip development deals with Meta Platforms and OpenAI followed. The Google business expanded. Broadcom landed near the boom’s red-hot center, doing something Nvidia’s general-purpose AI chips couldn’t.

 

The competitive circumstances have changed. While Broadcom was once Google’s sole partner in designing its TPUs, Google has since brought in Taiwan’s MediaTek.

 

Google also recently signed a long-term deal with Marvell Technology for networking and other custom chips. Marvell said the deal could bring in roughly $120 billion of revenue through its 2033 fiscal year. While that deal doesn’t compete directly with Broadcom’s TPUs, Google is charting a course that lessens its reliance on its partner.

 

The disadvantages of Broadcom’s AI-chip strategy are also coming into sharper focus as the financial capacity of the healthiest tech companies gets stretched.

 

The chips Broadcom is helping customers design are customized for specific computing work. That is, in one sense, an advantage over competitors like Nvidia, which offer more general-purpose chips. But it becomes a problem if one of Broadcom’s custom-chip customers falters. In that case, those chips and the designs behind them would be harder to transfer to a different customer.

 

Amid those shifts, Broadcom’s allure for investors is also changing.

 

Previously, it wasn’t all AI, all the time. About 44% of revenue came from AI chips in the first fiscal quarter of 2026, the first time it broke out those numbers. But that is set to rise to 70% within the next year, if analyst forecasts hold.

 

With all its challenges, Broadcom’s stock hasn’t been a great performer lately. It has risen 6% this year, while the PHLX Semiconductor Index is up 60%. Even so, Broadcom isn’t a bargain, priced at about 20 times forward earnings. That is slightly above the 19-times average for the PHLX and higher than Nvidia’s multiple of about 17 times.

 

Broadcom is riding high. Yet it still has much to prove.
